text: Assign input-stack ownership explicitly: device enablement (libinput/evdev/HID, keyboard layouts, gestures) in HW, routing and focus in UIP.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Define the clipboard authority policy: reads require a user paste gesture or an explicit grant, writes are always allowed, and clipboard history is a privileged shell feature rather than an ambient stream.
rationale: Silent clipboard reading is a common data-exfiltration vector and §41 lists clipboard capabilities without specifying the policy.

text: Right-to-left layout mirroring, locale-aware date/number/currency/collation APIs, and a target set of fully translated 1.0 languages with a published percent-translated gate.
rationale: 1.0 must define which users it actually serves and RTL mirroring is an architectural toolkit property, not a translation.

text: Clipboard policy ADR: no ambient clipboard read, reads permitted only on a user-initiated paste gesture into the focused surface or via an explicit Capability<ClipboardRead> for clipboard managers, with typed content negotiation and lazy transfer over MemoryObject.
rationale: Clipboard sniffing is the most common data-exfiltration path on existing desktops and the baseline lists clipboard capabilities without defining the policy.

text: Unified drag-and-drop and clipboard content types across native, Wayland/X11 (wl_data_device, XDND) and Windows (OLE) personalities, where a drop grants the target a capability to the dropped object rather than a path.
rationale: Dragging a file from a native file browser into a Windows app and vice versa is the litmus test for compat feeling native.

text: Decision that X11-style primary selection (middle-click paste) is not a native concept and exists only inside the Linux personality.
rationale: An explicit non-goal prevents a historical Unix behaviour from leaking into the native model per §68.

text: Appearance model: light/dark, accent colour, icon and cursor themes, wallpaper, and font scale exposed to native apps as typed settings and to Linux apps via the settings portal and GTK/Qt platform hints.
rationale: Inconsistent theming between native and compat windows is immediately visible and portals are the accepted channel for it.

text: Global shortcut model where apps request named actions bound by the user in Settings and never receive raw global key grabs.
rationale: Push-to-talk, screenshots, and media apps need global keys and the ambient X11 grab model is a keylogger primitive.

text: Basic touchscreen and touchpad gesture support ships, but on-screen keyboard, tablet mode, and convertible form-factor UI are explicitly out of scope for 1.0.
rationale: Constraining scope to desktop and laptop keeps §62's hardware target honest while still handling touchscreens present on target laptops.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Prototype the native UI protocol as retained scene graph transmitted over channels, client-rendered buffers, and a hybrid, and choose by measured latency, memory and toolkit ergonomics.
rationale: The UI protocol shape determines accessibility, automation and remote-surface capabilities and is nearly as permanent as the kernel ABI.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide whether to build a new UI toolkit or adopt and adapt an existing Rust toolkit and renderer, with an evaluation matrix covering accessibility tree output and declarative model fit.
rationale: Toolkit effort is a multi-year cost and must be scoped before the four V0.5 demo applications are started.

text: UI is a user-space service above native kernel objects (compositor, UI protocol).
A native application must not automatically receive clipboard access.
Define the UI capability that a launched application receives (window creation without screen contents).
Do not inherit X11 as any part of the native UI platform.
Do not make Wayland the native UI API.
Design and implement a new native UI protocol between applications and the compositor/shell.
Native UI platform must support declarative UI.
Native UI platform must support retained-mode rendering.
Native UI platform must support responsive layout.
Native UI platform must support GPU rendering.
Native UI platform must support animation with frame-scheduled updates.
Native UI platform must support input (pointer, keyboard, touch, pen, gamepad) delivered only to focused surfaces.
Native UI platform must support drag and drop, where a drop transfers a capability to the target (§9).
Native UI platform must implement clipboard as a capability (no ambient clipboard read, §9).
Native UI platform must support adaptive form factors (desktop, laptop, external display, future tablet).
Native UI platform must support high-DPI including mixed-DPI across displays.
Decide the UI protocol model: application ships a retained scene/element tree to the compositor, or renders into Buffers and ships surfaces (ADR).
Decide the native toolkit architecture and implementation language (Rust toolkit with bindings) (ADR).
Version the native UI protocol using the interface versioning rules of §12.
Study Flutter, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Slint and Xilem declarative models before fixing the native declarative UI model.
Provide a theming and styling system for native applications.
Decide server-side versus client-side window decorations for native and compatibility windows (ADR).
Implement a native keyboard shortcut and focus model that does not permit global key interception without a capability.
Do not expose Wayland as the native UI API.
Input delivery (keyboard, mouse, touchpad) through the native UI protocol to focused surfaces.
Basic declarative UI toolkit with retained rendering sufficient for the four demo applications (cross-ref §41).
